### Quiz 2: Working Scientifically – Questioning & Predicting; Hypotheses; Variables; Causation

1. Which statement is the best example of a testable, operationalised hypothesis?
- [ ] Plants grow better with more care.
- [x] Tomato plants watered with 50 mL of 0.5% nutrient solution daily will produce a greater mean mass of fruit over 8 weeks than plants watered with 50 mL of water daily.
- [ ] Nutrients are important for plants.
- [ ] Plants watered more grow faster.

2. In an investigation testing the effect of light intensity on algal growth, which is the independent variable?
- [x] Light intensity at the culture surface
- [ ] Mass of algae at the end of the week
- [ ] Temperature of room
- [ ] Volume of culture medium

3. A class compares two brands of thermometers by measuring the temperature of the same water bath five times with each. What is the primary purpose of this design?
- [ ] To increase validity
- [x] To compare precision of instruments
- [ ] To eliminate bias through blinding
- [ ] To standardise the independent variable

4. Which scenario most clearly supports a causal relationship rather than mere correlation?
- [ ] Ice cream sales and drowning incidents both rise in summer.
- [x] A randomized controlled trial shows participants given a specific sleep hygiene program sleep 45 minutes longer than controls, with all other factors controlled.
- [ ] A survey finds students who sit at the front have higher marks.
- [ ] A lab notes two variables increase together in the same dataset.

5. What is the best purpose of a negative control in an enzyme assay?
- [ ] To raise statistical power
- [x] To show the measured effect is not due to the assay reagents alone
- [ ] To increase the sample size of the treated group
- [ ] To confirm the hypothesis is true

6. Which statement correctly defines the null hypothesis (H0)?
- [ ] The hypothesis the researcher believes to be true
- [x] A statement that there is no effect or no difference between groups
- [ ] A prediction based on a model
- [ ] The outcome with the largest p-value

7. A student suggests, “Caffeine causes increased heart rate.” Which revision makes this claim more testable?
- [ ] Caffeine is bad for your heart.
- [x] A 200 mg dose of caffeine increases mean resting heart rate within 30 minutes compared to placebo in adults aged 18–25.
- [ ] People feel more awake after caffeine.
- [ ] Caffeine changes physiology.

8. Which change is most likely to increase the internal validity of an experiment?
- [ ] Increasing the sample size
- [ ] Repeating the experiment next month
- [x] Holding temperature, pH, and volume constant across treatments
- [ ] Publishing results in a journal

9. In a blind taste test for a new sports drink, which element reduces participant expectation effects?
- [ ] Using the same bottle for both drinks
- [x] Not telling participants which drink is the new formula
- [ ] Measuring heart rate before and after
- [ ] Giving participants a questionnaire

10. A teacher asks students to investigate if music tempo affects reaction time. Which is the dependent variable?
- [ ] Tempo of music
- [ ] Volume of music
- [x] Reaction time measured in milliseconds
- [ ] Brand of headphones

11. In a fair test, which variable should be deliberately changed?
- [x] Independent variable
- [ ] Dependent variable
- [ ] Controlled variable
- [ ] Confounding variable

12. Which question aligns best with the “questioning and predicting” stage?
- [ ] How will we calibrate the balance?
- [x] What effect will increasing salinity have on the germination rate of radish seeds?
- [ ] What is the most ethical way to store data?
- [ ] How should we present the results?

13. A claim that “students who chew gum score higher on exams” is made from an observational study. Which is the most plausible confounder?
- [x] Gum chewers may study more frequently
- [ ] The flavour of gum causes memory changes
- [ ] Gum changes exam difficulty
- [ ] The exam room temperature rises when gum is chewed

14. Which action primarily improves reliability?
- [x] Repeating measurements under the same conditions
- [ ] Replacing the hypothesis with a new one
- [ ] Increasing the effect size
- [ ] Publishing negative results

15. Which best distinguishes accuracy from precision?
- [ ] Accuracy is repeatability; precision is closeness to true value
- [x] Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is repeatability
- [ ] Accuracy is validity; precision is reliability
- [ ] Accuracy is causation; precision is correlation

16. A digital scale reads 0.15 g when empty. What type of error is this most likely?
- [ ] Random
- [x] Systematic zero error
- [ ] Blinding error
- [ ] Sampling error

17. A student wants to detect a small effect of a nutrient on plant growth. Which design change most increases the chance of detecting it?
- [ ] Use a less sensitive instrument
- [x] Increase sample size with random assignment to groups
- [ ] Reduce replication
- [ ] Eliminate the control group

18. Which statement about placebo controls is correct?
- [ ] They control for random error
- [ ] They calibrate instruments
- [x] They control for the psychological effect of receiving a treatment
- [ ] They increase external validity

19. Which situation most clearly shows overgeneralisation?
- [ ] Reporting an outlier
- [ ] Using a stratified sample
- [x] Concluding all teenagers prefer energy drinks after surveying one class
- [ ] Reporting a confidence interval

20. What is the primary reason to conduct a pilot study?
- [ ] To increase statistical significance
- [x] To test and refine procedures and instruments before the main study
- [ ] To replace the need for controls
- [ ] To ensure the hypothesis is correct

### Quiz 3: Planning & Conducting – Experimental Design; Sampling; Risk; Ethics

1. Which change best improves the representativeness of a field sample of leaf litter in a forest?
- [ ] Sampling only near the trail for convenience
- [x] Using a stratified random sample across canopy cover types
- [ ] Doubling the number of samples in one clearing
- [ ] Sampling only large leaves

2. Which is the correct order in the hierarchy of controls for risk management (most to least effective)?
- [x] Elimination, substitution, engineering controls, administrative controls, PPE
- [ ] PPE, elimination, substitution, administrative, engineering
- [ ] Substitution, elimination, administrative, PPE, engineering
- [ ] Administrative, engineering, elimination, PPE, substitution

3. When planning to measure dissolved oxygen in a stream, which step most improves accuracy?
- [ ] Taking fewer readings
- [x] Calibrating the probe with fresh standards at field temperature
- [ ] Avoiding field notes to save time

4. Which scenario most clearly breaches informed consent?

- [ ] Providing an information sheet and allowing students to opt out
- [ ] Allowing parental consent for minors
- [ ] Storing de-identified data securely

5. A team sets quadrats along a transect from shore to deeper water to study species distribution. What sampling method is this?
- [ ] Random sampling
- [ ] Stratified random sampling
- [x] Systematic sampling along a gradient (transect)
- [ ] Convenience sampling

6. In an investigation of fertilizer types, which is the best control?
- [x] Plants grown with identical conditions but no fertilizer
- [ ] Plants watered twice as much
- [ ] Plants placed closer to the window
- [ ] Plants with a different soil type

7. Which action best prevents contamination between microbial culture plates?

- [ ] Opening lids widely to speed up plating
- [ ] Touching agar with ungloved hands
- [ ] Incubating plates at 37°C in an unlabelled stack

8. What is the safest way to transport corrosive acid for a school experiment?
- [ ] In a glass beaker with no lid
- [ ] In any container to reduce cost
- [ ] In a student’s backpack
- [x] In a labelled, sealed chemical transport bottle in a secondary containment tray

9. Which step is required to ensure repeatability when measuring time to complete a reaction?
- [x] Use the same defined end-point and timing method across repeats
- [ ] Have each student choose their own end-point
- [ ] Change the timer for each trial
- [ ] Record time only when the result is “interesting”

10. Which aspect of an SDS (Safety Data Sheet) is most relevant when deciding PPE?
- [x] Hazard identification and recommended protective equipment
- [ ] Manufacturer’s phone number
- [ ] Date of purchase
- [ ] Storage location in the lab

11. For a double-blind clinical-style school simulation, blinding means:
- [ ] Only participants are unaware of treatment allocation
- [x] Both participants and data collectors are unaware of treatment allocation
- [ ] Only the teacher is aware of allocation
- [ ] Everyone knows who got the treatment

12. Which practice best ensures traceability of samples?
- [ ] Labelling after analysis
- [x] Unique sample IDs recorded in a bound logbook at collection
- [ ] Colour-coding caps without a key
- [ ] Relying on memory

13. A field study occurs near culturally significant sites. Which action best aligns with ethical and respectful practice?
- [x] Consult relevant Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander community representatives before planning and obtain permissions
- [ ] Proceed without consultation to avoid delays
- [ ] Keep locations secret from everyone
- [ ] Only consult after collecting samples

14. Which statement about replication and repeats is correct?
- [ ] Repeats are different labs duplicating the study; replication is same lab doing it again
- [x] Repeats are repeated measurements within the same study; replication is independent repetition by others
- [ ] Replication and repeats are the same
- [ ] Replication does not improve reliability

15. Which is the best justification for using a placebo control in a study of a cognitive supplement?
- [ ] To reduce sample size
- [x] To control for expectation and placebo effects
- [ ] To eliminate confounding completely
- [ ] To prove causation without statistics

16. When preparing a 0.100 M NaCl solution, which action most improves accuracy?
- [x] Using an analytical balance and dissolving to volume in a volumetric flask
- [ ] Estimating mass with a scoop
- [ ] Dissolving in a beaker to approximate volume
- [ ] Recording mass to 1 g only

17. Which factor most strongly affects external validity?
- [ ] Calibrating the instrument
- [x] How representative the sample and conditions are of the target population and context
- [ ] Repeating measurements within the same sample
- [ ] Using blinding

18. A risk assessment identifies a hazard with low likelihood but severe consequence. Which response is most appropriate?
- [x] Implement strong controls to reduce consequence and/or likelihood despite low probability
- [ ] Ignore due to low likelihood
- [ ] Rely solely on PPE
- [ ] Cancel the entire investigation without considering controls

19. Which is the most appropriate method to sample fast-moving insects in a grassland?
- [ ] Quadrat counts only
- [ ] Soil core sampling
- [x] Sweep netting along transects with timed effort
- [ ] Pitfall traps in a single location

20. When human participants are involved, which is essential?
- [x] Informed consent and the right to withdraw without penalty
- [ ] Mandatory participation if anonymised
- [ ] Collecting names for verification
- [ ] Publishing raw identifiable data

### Quiz 4: Processing & Analysing – Data, Uncertainty, Graphs, Statistics

1. A balance has a resolution of 0.01 g. What is the best estimate of reading uncertainty for a single mass measurement?
- [ ] ±0.01 g
- [x] ±0.005 g
- [ ] ±0.1 g
- [ ] ±0.0005 g

2. Which statistic is least affected by outliers?
- [ ] Mean
- [x] Median
- [ ] Range
- [ ] Standard deviation

3. A scatter plot shows a strong negative linear trend. Which is the most appropriate model to test first?
- [x] Linear regression with negative slope
- [ ] Quadratic with positive curvature
- [ ] Exponential growth model
- [ ] No model; assume no relationship

4. If two measurements are added, what happens to their absolute uncertainties?
- [x] They add
- [ ] They subtract
- [ ] They multiply
- [ ] They remain unchanged

5. Which graphing choice is most misleading?
- [ ] Including error bars
- [x] Truncating the y-axis to start just below the smallest bar to exaggerate differences without disclosure
- [ ] Labelling axes with units
- [ ] Including a trendline with R²

6. A dataset is positively skewed. Which measure best represents central tendency?
- [ ] Mean only
- [x] Median
- [ ] Mode only
- [ ] Range

7. A correlation coefficient r = 0.02 (p = 0.89). What is the correct interpretation?
- [ ] Strong positive correlation
- [ ] Strong negative correlation
- [x] No evidence of a linear relationship
- [ ] Causation is confirmed

8. Which step is most appropriate when encountering a clear outlier due to a known instrument fault?

9. When should a log transformation of the y-variable be considered?
- [ ] When the relationship is already linear
- [x] When growth appears exponential and variance increases with the mean
- [ ] When units are incorrect
- [ ] When the sample size is small

10. Two independent measurements are multiplied. How should relative (percentage) uncertainties be treated?
- [x] They add
- [ ] They subtract
- [ ] They remain unchanged
- [ ] They average

11. A 95% confidence interval for the mean mass is 12.4 to 13.0 g. What does this mean?

12. Which situation indicates high precision but low accuracy?

13. Which is the best reason to use a box-and-whisker plot?
- [x] To compare medians and interquartile ranges across groups
- [ ] To show individual time series
- [ ] To display a calibration curve
- [ ] To present categorical proportions

14. The slope of a calibration line is 2.50 AU per mg/L (intercept ≈ 0). A sample reads 1.00 AU. What is its concentration?
- [x] 0.40 mg/L

- [ ] 0.25 mg/L

15. What is the most appropriate action when residuals from a linear fit show curvature?

- [x] Consider a different model (e.g., quadratic) or transform variables

16. A study compares two groups with overlapping error bars. What is the correct conclusion?
- [ ] The groups are significantly different
- [x] Overlap suggests differences may not be statistically significant; further analysis is needed
- [ ] The groups are identical
- [ ] The sample size is too large

17. When is interpolation generally more reliable than extrapolation?
- [x] Within the range of observed data
- [ ] Beyond the range of observed data

- [ ] Only when the sample size is > 100

18. A student rounds every intermediate calculation to 2 significant figures. What is the likely effect?

- [ ] Increased accuracy
- [ ] Improved validity
- [ ] Reduced bias

19. What does a high R² (e.g., 0.95) guarantee?

- [x] A strong proportion of variance explained by the model; not necessarily causation

20. Which test is most appropriate to compare means of two independent groups with approximately normal data and similar variances?

### Quiz 5: Models, Theories and Laws – Nature of Science; Validation; Limitations

1. Which statement best distinguishes a scientific law from a theory?
- [ ] A law explains; a theory describes
- [x] A law describes a consistent relationship; a theory explains mechanisms underlying observations
- [ ] Laws are guesses; theories are proven facts

2. Which is the best description of a model in science?

- [x] A simplified representation used to explain, predict, or test ideas

- [ ] A collection of untested opinions

3. An analogy model of an atom is like a solar system. Which is a key limitation?
- [x] Electrons do not orbit like planets; quantum behavior is not captured
- [ ] The nucleus is too small
- [ ] Models cannot use analogies
- [ ] Atoms have moons

4. What provides the strongest support that a model is useful?
- [ ] It is widely taught
- [ ] It is aesthetically pleasing
- [x] It makes accurate, testable predictions across conditions
- [ ] It uses complex mathematics

5. When a model consistently overestimates values at high inputs, which approach is most appropriate?
- [x] Re-examine assumptions; recalibrate or choose a model that accounts for saturation or nonlinearity
- [ ] Ignore the discrepancy

- [ ] Publish as is

6. A theory persists despite anomalies. Which is the best scientific response?

- [ ] Dismiss anomalies as noise
- [ ] Abandon the theory immediately
- [ ] Keep collecting the same data indefinitely

7. Which example best shows falsifiability?
- [x] “Under standard conditions, increasing pressure decreases gas volume.”

- [ ] “The universe prefers symmetry.”

8. Overfitting is most likely when:

- [x] The model has too many parameters relative to the data, fitting noise

9. Which statement about paradigm shifts is most accurate?

- [ ] They are purely political

10. What is sensitivity analysis in modelling?

- [x] Evaluating how model outputs change when inputs or parameters vary
- [ ] Testing for blinding
- [ ] Comparing means across groups

11. Why are assumptions explicitly stated in models?
- [x] To clarify scope, limitations, and conditions where the model is valid
- [ ] To hide weaknesses
- [ ] To increase complexity
- [ ] To replace data collection

12. Which provides the strongest evidence for a computational climate model’s validity?
- [ ] Agreement with a single year’s data
- [ ] Public popularity
- [x] Skill in hindcasting past climate and predicting independent future observations
- [ ] Complexity of code

13. Which best differentiates empirical and mechanistic models?
- [x] Empirical models fit observed patterns; mechanistic models incorporate causal processes
- [ ] Mechanistic models ignore mechanisms

- [ ] Mechanistic models cannot predict

14. In model evaluation, what does cross-validation primarily assess?
- [ ] Internal validity
- [x] Predictive performance on unseen data
- [ ] Ethical compliance
- [ ] Instrument precision

15. A scale model of a bridge is built at 1:100 size. Which is a key consideration?
- [x] Dynamic similarity (e.g., Reynolds number) may not scale linearly
- [ ] Materials need not be considered
- [ ] Gravity has no effect at small scales
- [ ] Scaling removes uncertainty

16. Which is the best reason to update a model after new evidence emerges?
- [x] To improve explanatory power and predictive accuracy
- [ ] To match public expectations
- [ ] To increase complexity for status
- [ ] To avoid peer review

17. Which is an example of a scientific law?
- [x] The relationship between pressure and volume for a gas at constant temperature (Boyle’s law)
- [ ] The cell theory
- [ ] The theory of evolution by natural selection
- [ ] The plate tectonics theory

18. A student claims a model is valid because it fits the calibration data perfectly (R² = 1). What is the best critique?
- [x] It may be overfit; check predictive performance on independent data
- [ ] Perfect fit always proves causation

- [ ] Complexity ensures validity

19. Why are multiple, independent lines of evidence valued when evaluating theories?

- [ ] It makes conclusions less reliable

- [ ] It replaces the need for replication

20. Which is an acceptable role of a model even if it is not “true” in all details?
